strengths: Clear problem identification: the paper convincingly motivates why BN moving statistics are unreliable in online RL (non-stationary data distribution) and why this matters specifically for SNNs, where BN is indispensable for stable training.

Principled method design: the confidence-adaptive update (Ca-BN) is derived from a Kalman-style MSE-optimal linear combination of two estimators (Theorem 1 with proof), and the re-calibration (Re-BN) mechanism is a practical, computationally cheap alternative to full dataset re-estimation.

Zero inference overhead: CaRe-BN only modifies how training-time moving statistics are estimated, so the deployment cost/energy profile of the SNN is preserved — an important practical property for the neuromorphic use case.

Comprehensive experimental protocol: five MuJoCo environments, two RL algorithms (DDPG, TD3), two neuron models (LIF, CLIF), comparisons against SOTA SNN-RL methods (pop-SAN, MDC-SAN, ILC-SAN, ANN-SNN conversion) and against SNN-specific BN variants (tdBN, BNTT, TEBN, TABN), plus ablations of both components and an ANN control experiment (Fig. 5d) that helps rule out a generic RL-boosting effect.

Additional analysis beyond final return: exploration performance (Fig. 3), variance reduction across seeds (Fig. 5a,b), and consistency of gains across algorithm/neuron combinations support the main claims.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in isolation: the Ca-BN update is essentially a Kalman-filter-style adaptive-EMA for running statistics, and Re-BN is a periodic re-estimation with larger aggregated batches (explicitly following Wu & Johnson 2021). Both ideas are known in other contexts; the contribution is their adaptation to SNN-RL, which is solid but incremental.

The theoretical derivation rests on questionable assumptions that are not discussed: (i) Theorem 1 implicitly assumes the previous estimate and the current batch statistic are independent, but the moving average is built from past overlapping batches; (ii) the proxy D(µ*i − µ̂i|i−1) ≈ Dµi in Eq. 11-12 conflates distribution drift with estimation noise in the squared error (µi − µ̂i−1)², so the 'unbiasedness and optimal variance reduction' claim is not strictly established for the actual estimator used; (iii) the Gaussian activation assumption in Assumption 1 may be poor for spiking activations.

Statistical support for the headline claim is weak: the 5.9% APG over the ANN baseline is dominated by IDP-v4 (9348 vs. 7503), where the ANN baseline has an enormous standard deviation (±3713) over only 5 seeds; on HalfCheetah the ANN actually outperforms CaRe-BN (10857 vs. 9563). No significance tests are reported, so 'SNNs surpass ANNs by 5.9%' is likely within noise.

Scope of evaluation is narrow: only DDPG and TD3 (no SAC/PPO), only low-dimensional MuJoCo locomotion, no real neuromorphic hardware deployment or energy measurements despite the energy-efficiency motivation, and no demonstration on harder/high-dimensional tasks.
Missing sensitivity analysis for the new hyperparameters (momentum α, calibration batch count M, recalibration interval Tcal), which directly govern the noise–delay trade-off the paper centers on.
Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, and key details (architecture, hyperparameters, replay buffer size) are deferred to an appendix not included in the main text.
Presentation issues: typos ('Ture' in Fig. 1 legend, 'Dispite'), duplicate references (Lillicrap; Todorov; Mnih), and Figure 2 is difficult to parse without more explanation.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and underexplored problem: Batch Normalization's moving statistics are unreliable under the nonstationary data distribution of online RL, which is particularly acute for directly trained SNNs that depend heavily on BN.

The proposed method (CaRe-BN) is lightweight, does not change inference-time computation, and is claimed to be a drop-in replacement, which is attractive from a deployment/energy-efficiency standpoint.

The experimental suite is reasonably broad in one dimension: two RL algorithms (DDPG, TD3) and two neuron models (LIF, CLIF) across five MuJoCo tasks, with comparisons to several SNN-specific BN variants (tdBN, BNTT, TEBN, TABN) and SNN-RL methods (pop-SAN, MDC-SAN, ILC-SAN).

Ablation studies separating the confidence-adaptive update (Ca-BN) and re-calibration (Re-BN) are provided, and the ANN control experiment (Section 5.6) is a useful check against the alternative explanation that the gains come from a generic RL improvement.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core of Ca-BN is a Kalman-style optimal linear combination of two estimators (Eq. 5-6), which is a textbook result, and closely mirrors existing work on Kalman-based normalization for nonstationary settings (e.g., Kalman Normalization, NeurIPS 2018), which is not cited or compared. Re-BN is essentially the periodic BN recalibration of Wu & Johnson (2021) applied with replay-buffer batches. The paper claims to be 'the first BN method specifically designed for SNNs in RL,' but this framing underplays these direct precedents.

The theoretical analysis is heuristic and does not support the strong claims. Theorem 1 is a standard MSE-optimal linear combination result under an unbiasedness assumption that is itself questionable under distribution drift: the previous estimate µ̂_{i|i-1} is not unbiased for µ*_i when the distribution shifts, violating the premise of the proof. The approximations in Eqs. 9-12 (replacing unknown drift variance with recursively smoothed squared differences) are ad hoc and their effect is not analyzed.

Evaluation has several concerns. (i) Only 5 random seeds and 'max average returns' are reported, an optimistic aggregation; combined with the large variances (e.g., ANN on IDP-v4: 7503 ± 3713), the 5.9% APG claim is not convincingly supported. (ii) IDP-v4 appears saturated (all methods ~9350 ± 1-2), inflating the apparent competitiveness of many baselines. (iii) The headline 'improves performance by up to 22.6%' is a best-case number not clearly substantiated in the main text, and the gains are concentrated on Ant-v4 and Hopper-v4; HalfCheetah and Walker2d show marginal or no gains over TABN.

Missing baselines: no comparison against vanilla BN with a tuned momentum (a strong, trivially simple baseline given the paper's own 'noise-delay trade-off' framing), no comparison to Kalman Normalization or other online/adaptive normalization methods, and no offline evaluation on actual neuromorphic hardware or any energy measurements, despite energy efficiency being the central motivation.

The significance of the contribution is undermined by the paper's own Section 5.6: CaRe-BN provides no benefit on ANNs, so the contribution is confined to the narrow niche of SNN + BN + off-policy RL. This niche-specific effect is acknowledged but not explored in depth (e.g., why CLIF vs LIF differ drastically in variance in Fig. 5).

Presentation and rigor issues: typos ('Ture' in Figure 1 legend, 'Dispite' in Section 5.6), duplicated references (Lillicrap 2015 appears twice; Todorov 2014a and 2014b are identical; Mnih 2015a/b and 2013 are redundant), and inconsistencies between the text and Figure 5 (the text cites ANN baseline variances of 17.71%/21.24% that do not match the figure's scale). The ablation results in Fig. 5(c) are only shown as normalized percentages without raw returns or statistical tests.

Reproducibility is unclear: key details (network architecture, α, N, M, T_cal, replay buffer sizes) are deferred to an appendix not provided, and no code release is mentioned. The claim that the computational overhead of Re-BN 'remains negligible' is asserted rather than measured (no wall-clock or throughput comparison).

The claim that 'CaRe-BN does not alter inference' is misleading in the sense that Re-BN does overwrite the statistics used at inference; the accurate statement is that inference machinery is unchanged, not that inference behavior is unaffected.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: BN moving-statistics imprecision in nonstationary online RL is a real bottleneck for directly-trained SNNs, and the paper explains both the noise–delay trade-off (fast vs. slow EMA momentum) and why supervised-learning BN variants do not transfer to RL.

Clean, principled method design: the confidence-adaptive (Ca-BN) update is derived as a Kalman-style optimal MSE-weighted combination of the previous estimate and the current mini-batch statistics, with the estimation variances derived from standard sampling theory (Eqs. 8–12), and the periodic Re-BN recalibration (Eq. 13) is a practical, low-cost surrogate for exact dataset-wide BN recomputation.

No inference overhead: CaRe-BN leaves inference identical to vanilla BN, preserving the energy-efficiency argument for neuromorphic deployment — an important practical property often violated by other BN variants (BNTT, TEBN, etc.).

Broad empirical evaluation: 5 MuJoCo continuous-control tasks, 2 RL algorithms (DDPG, TD3), 2 neuron models (LIF, CLIF), comparisons against SOTA SNN-RL methods (pop-SAN, MDC-SAN, ILC-SAN, ANN-SNN conversion) and SNN BN variants (tdBN, BNTT, TEBN, TABN), with 5 seeds, reported standard deviations, and an APG metric.

Useful ablations (Ca-BN vs. Re-BN vs. combined) and a thoughtful control experiment showing CaRe-BN does not help shallow ANNs, supporting the claim that gains stem from SNN-specific normalization rather than an implicit RL improvement; also demonstrates reduced training variance.
Strong headline result: SNNs with CaRe-BN surpass the ANN TD3 baseline on average (+5.9% APG), which is notable for the SNN-RL sub-area.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core of Ca-BN is a standard Kalman-filter gain applied to EMA statistics, and Re-BN is essentially precise-BN (Wu & Johnson, 2021) applied periodically to replay-buffer samples. The contribution is a sensible combination of known techniques tailored to SNN-RL rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The theoretical derivation is thinner than presented: the variance of the previous estimate (Eq. 11–12) is a heuristic recursively-smoothed proxy rather than a rigorous estimator, the unbiasedness of the previous-estimate term is not established under distribution drift, and the Gaussianity assumption (Assumption 1) is certainly violated by spiking activations; no analysis of the resulting bias or robustness is given.

Some experimental concerns: only 5 random seeds for high-variance RL; DDPG results in Ant-v4 are omitted due to divergence (unclear how this is handled in aggregates); APG averaging masks environment-level weaknesses (e.g., HalfCheetah 9563 vs. 10857 for the ANN baseline); the headline ANN comparison uses a normalization-free ANN TD3, and it is not shown whether BN in ANNs with proper statistics would close the gap.

Missing analyses: no sensitivity study for the new hyperparameters (momentum α, recalibration interval T_cal, number of calibration batches M), no wall-clock/compute overhead measurements for the periodic recalibration, and no direct measurement that BN statistics are actually closer to the ground-truth population statistics (the motivating claim in Figure 1 is only qualitatively illustrated).

Evaluation scope is narrow: only DDPG/TD3 on MuJoCo; no on-policy algorithms (PPO/SAC would stress-test the claims about nonstationarity differently), no sim-to-real or energy measurements to substantiate the neuromorphic deployment narrative, and it is not fully specified where BN is applied (actor only? critic?) in the hybrid ANN-critic setup.

Clarity issues: Figure 1 typos ('Ture'), 'Dispite' in Section 5.6, duplicated references (Lillicrap 2015, Mnih 2015a/b, Todorov 2014a/b), and the ablation metric 'normalized maximum performance' (Fig. 5c) is not precisely defined; no explicit code-release statement weakens reproducibility.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement: the noise–delay trade-off of BN moving statistics under nonstationary online RL dynamics is a real and underexplored issue, and it is especially relevant for SNNs that critically depend on normalization for stable surrogate-gradient training.

The confidence-adaptive update (Ca-BN) has a principled derivation as an optimal linear combination of two unbiased estimators (Theorem 1), inspired by Kalman filtering, with the two components (Ca-BN and Re-BN) complementary and individually ablated (Fig. 6c).

Extensive empirical evaluation: multiple RL algorithms (DQN, DDPG, TD3, SAC), multiple spiking neuron models (LIF, CLIF, DN), both continuous control (MuJoCo) and discrete control (Atari), comparisons against SOTA SNN-RL methods (pop-SAN, MDC-SAN, ILC-SAN) and SNN-specific BN variants (tdBN, BNTT, TEBN, TABN).

Good supporting analyses: Wasserstein distance between estimated and true statistics (Fig. 3), exploration return improvements (Fig. 4), variance reduction, training-time/memory overhead (Table 20), and inference energy estimates (Table 21), which substantiate the 'no inference overhead / energy-preserving' claim.

Results that SNNs with CaRe-BN exceed ANN baselines (5.90% APG) plus the simulation-time-step study (Table 17) and ANN control experiment (Fig. 6d) strengthen the significance of the contribution and rule out a generic RL-mechanism explanation.
Reproducibility is well supported: full hyperparameter tables for all algorithms and neuron models, architecture details, and stated code availability.
weaknesses: Technical soundness of Theorem 1 is weaker than presented: the variance decomposition in Eq. (7) implicitly assumes the two estimators are independent, but the prior estimate μ̂_{i|i−1} is built from past batches that are correlated with the current minibatch statistics, so the optimal K is not exactly as derived. The approximations in Eqs. (9)–(11) (using squared deviations as 'unbiased probes' of the drift variance, then EMA-smoothing them) are heuristic and their quality is never quantified.

The Gaussianity assumption on activations (Assumption 1) is questionable for spiking networks, where layer outputs are sums of binary spikes and often far from Gaussian; no empirical validation of this assumption or sensitivity analysis is provided.

The headline result is fragile in places: gains on IDP-v4 are near-ceiling and negligible (9348 vs 9346 for tdBN), most improvement concentrates on Ant/Walker2d, and the ANN baseline on IDP is anomalously low with huge variance (7503 ± 3713), which inflates the 5.9% APG claim. DDPG divergence on Ant-v4 removes that comparison entirely. Only 5 seeds (3 for Atari) are used.

Novelty is moderate: adaptive fusion of an EMA prior with a fresh noisy sample is essentially a Kalman update / adaptive-momentum heuristic, and Re-BN (recomputing statistics from replay buffer resampling) is a straightforward extension of the recalibration idea in Wu & Johnson (2021). A simpler baseline such as a tuned momentum sweep for vanilla BN, or other adaptive-momentum schemes, is missing and would be needed to justify the added complexity.

The claim that exploration improvement is 'solely due to more precise estimation of BN statistics' (Sec. 5.2) is a causal claim supported only by correlational evidence (Wasserstein distance and exploration returns both improving); a direct intervention or correlation analysis between estimation error and per-episode returns would be more convincing.

Presentation issues: several typos ('Dispite', 'Dynnamic', 'niose'), duplicated Lillicrap (2015) references, a future-dated citation (arXiv:2601.21778, 2026), and Figure 1's claimed contrast between (a)/(b) and (c)/(d) is only loosely supported by the schematic illustration rather than measured data.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and underexplored problem: BatchNorm moving-statistics estimation breaks down under the non-stationary data distributions of online RL, and this is especially relevant for SNNs, which depend heavily on normalization for stable surrogate-gradient training.

The proposed method is lightweight and inference-preserving (fusable into synaptic weights), so it genuinely maintains the energy-efficiency motivation of SNN-RL; training overhead and GPU memory are explicitly measured (Table 20).

Experimental coverage is reasonably broad: DQN on Atari, DDPG/TD3/SAC on MuJoCo, three spiking neuron models (LIF, CLIF, DN), comparisons against several SNN-specific BN variants (tdBN, BNTT, TEBN, TABN) and direct-training SOTA methods (pop-SAN, MDC-SAN, ILC-SAN), plus an ablation separating Ca-BN and Re-BN.

Supporting analyses go beyond headline returns: Wasserstein distance to the true feature distribution (Fig. 3), exploration returns (Fig. 4), variance reduction (Fig. 6a,b), simulation-time-step sensitivity (Table 17), and energy consumption estimates (Table 21).
Reproducibility materials appear thorough: full hyperparameter tables for all algorithms, neuron parameters, architecture details, and a code availability statement.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin and the derivations are loose. Theorem 1 is essentially the standard BLUE/Kalman combination rule. More problematically, the claim that squared deviations (µi − µ̂i|i−1)² are 'unbiased but noisy probes' of D(µ*i − µ̂i|i−1) is incorrect in general: E[(µi − µ̂i|i−1)²] = Var(µi) + (bias of µ̂)², so these probes conflate estimation variance with drift-induced bias, and the estimator in Eq. 11 is itself a squared term updated by EMA, whose statistical properties are not analyzed. The Gaussianity and independence assumptions are never validated for actual activation distributions in the RL setting.

Novelty is moderate. Both components are direct adaptations of existing ideas: Kalman/confidence-weighted EMA is standard estimation theory, and the periodic recalibration from large stored samples closely mirrors PreciseBN (Wu & Johnson, 2021), which the authors cite. The contribution is largely an application/engineering combination tailored to SNN-RL rather than a new technique.

The recalibration mechanism raises an unaddressed distributional concern: replay-buffer samples are drawn from an old, off-policy data distribution, so recalibrating inference statistics on buffer data may bias them away from the current policy's activation distribution—precisely the non-stationarity problem the paper claims to solve. This mismatch is neither discussed nor empirically isolated (the ablation does not test recalibration on fresh on-policy batches).

Important design details of BN integration into the RL pipeline are missing: how BN statistics are handled in target networks (critical for TD3/DDPG), whether actor and critic use BN, and how recalibration interacts with target-network updates.

The headline claim that SNNs 'surpass their ANN counterparts by 5.9%' rests on a weak baseline: the ANN TD3 result on IDP-v4 is 7503 ± 3713, an enormous variance suggesting an unstable or mistuned baseline, and the APG metric is dominated by this single environment. Table 19 also shows CaRe-BN slightly *hurts* the ANN baseline (−0.69%), contradicting the claim that it 'does not negatively impact the RL training process.' No statistical significance tests are reported anywhere.

The evaluation is skewed by a saturated task (all methods score ~9350 on IDP-v4, rendering it uninformative) and a very small Atari evaluation (only 4 games, 3 random seeds), which limits the generality claims for discrete control.

The paper claims to be 'the first batch normalization method specifically designed for SNNs in RL,' but this claim is not carefully defended against related work on adaptive/online BN momentum in non-stationary or continual learning settings.

Presentation and rigor issues undermine confidence: duplicated and erroneous references (Lillicrap listed twice; a citation dated 'arXiv 2601.21778, 2026'), a table mislabeling ('Vanilla SNN' in the DDPG-with-ANN section, Table 18), typos ('Dispite', 'niose', 'DYNNAMIC'), and inconsistent notation in the proof (unbalanced parentheses in Eq. 11).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and previously unexplored problem: batch normalization in SNN-based online RL is poorly conditioned by nonstationary data distributions, while SNNs critically depend on normalization for stable surrogate-gradient training. This is a well-motivated niche with practical significance for neuromorphic RL.

The proposed method is technically sensible and lightweight: a Kalman-inspired confidence-weighted update of BN moving statistics plus a periodic replay-buffer-based recalibration. Importantly, it does not change inference, so it preserves SNN energy efficiency and is a drop-in replacement.

Evaluation is fairly broad for this subfield: four RL algorithms (DQN, DDPG, TD3, SAC), three spiking neuron models (LIF, CLIF, DN), both discrete (Atari) and continuous (MuJoCo) control, comparisons against SOTA SNN-RL methods (pop-SAN, MDC-SAN, ILC-SAN) and SNN-specific BN variants (tdBN, BNTT, TEBN, TABN), plus ablations of both components.

The analysis of *why* the method works (Figure 3 Wasserstein distance measurements, Figure 4 exploration returns) provides mechanistic evidence beyond raw score improvements, supporting the claimed statistics-to-exploration causal chain.

Practical deployment considerations are addressed with training-time/memory measurements and estimated inference energy consumption, and hyperparameters are consistent across settings; code and full configurations are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical framing has weaknesses. Theorem 1's optimal weighting requires D(μ*−μ̂_{i|i−1}), but the paper approximates it with the squared deviation (μ_i − μ̂_{i−1})², which conflates one noisy realization with the prior estimate's variance; the resulting estimator's actual MSE-optimality is not established under this substitution. Additionally, the notation in Theorem 1 (adaptive weights K^μ, K^σ) is inconsistent with the direct-weighted form used in Algorithm 1 line 5, and the D estimates and the statistics themselves are updated with the same EMA momentum, creating circularity that is not analyzed.

The headline claim that SNNs surpass ANNs by 5.9% rests heavily on InvertedDoublePendulum, where all SNN variants saturate at ~9350±1 while the ANN baseline achieves only 7503 with very large variance (±3713). On most other tasks the ANN is equal or better (e.g., HalfCheetah 10857 vs. 9563). This suggests the ANN baseline may be under-tuned or that the task is saturated, so the 'SNNs beat ANNs' narrative is stronger than the evidence.

Experimental diversity is limited: only 5 Atari games with 3 seeds (many learning curves overlap substantially, e.g., Breakout, SpaceInvaders), and DDPG on Ant is excluded because it diverges for both ANN and SNN. Several MuJoCo comparisons show overlapping confidence intervals, and no statistical significance tests are reported.

The derived confidence weights are sensitive to the approximations in Eq. 9–11, and no sensitivity analysis over the momentum α or recalibration frequency T_cal is provided; it is unclear how brittle the method is to these hyperparameters, which were fixed globally.

Some results lack a satisfying explanation: e.g., ANN+CaRe-BN is roughly neutral (Section 5.6), which is consistent with the method being SNN-specific but also leaves open whether gains come purely from a better-conditioned optimization regime rather than the specific estimator design.

Writing quality issues remain: typos ('DYNNAMIC', 'Dispite', 'batchs', 'niose'), duplicate Lillicrap references, and a citation with an impossible future date (arXiv:2601.21778, 2026), which undermines polish and citation care.

The scope of the theoretical claim ('unbiasedness and optimal variance reduction') overstates what is actually proven given the Gaussian assumption, the plug-in approximations, and the nonstationarity of RL data that violates the estimator assumptions.
